title: {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} vs {chip:atmel-t5577:name}: 125 kHz Chip Comparison
summary: A detailed technical comparison of the {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} read-only and {chip:atmel-t5577:name} read/write 125 kHz RFID chips. Covering memory architecture, modulation schemes, security features, cloning risks and migration paths for B2B access-control and identification deployments.
heroPoints: {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} is a read-only chip with a factory-programmed 40-bit ID. Simple, inexpensive and widely deployed but offering zero security against cloning.

{chip:atmel-t5577:name} provides 330 bits of rewritable memory and can emulate {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name}, HID Prox and other 125 kHz formats, making it the standard for multi-format and cloneable card applications.
Understanding the security limitations of both chips is critical for B2B buyers evaluating whether to upgrade legacy 125 kHz systems to 13.56 MHz smart cards.

sections.title: What does the 125 kHz RFID chip landscape look like?
sections.intro: The 125 kHz frequency band was the foundation of proximity-based identification from the 1990s through the early 2010s. Despite the security advantages of 13.56 MHz smart cards, 125 kHz systems remain in active production across access control, animal identification, industrial asset tracking and time-and-attendance applications due to installed-base inertia and lower per-tag cost.

image.alt: {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} and {chip:atmel-t5577:name} 125 kHz RFID access control cards

paragraphs: EM Microelectronic's [{chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name}](/guides/em4100-em4305-t5577-lf-chip-encyclopedia/) (also sold as EM4102) and Atmel's {chip:atmel-t5577:name} (now Microchip ATA5577) are the two most common 125 kHz chips in the B2B channel. They serve fundamentally different roles: {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} is a fixed-code transponder for simple identification, while {chip:atmel-t5577:name} is a programmable transponder that can store custom data and emulate multiple legacy chip formats.

callout.label: Migration path
callout.text: {chip:atmel-t5577:name} can emulate {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} and HID Prox formats, making it a versatile upgrade for legacy 125 kHz access control systems without replacing readers.

sections.title: How do memory architecture and data format work?
sections.intro: Understanding the internal memory layout of each chip clarifies what data can be stored, modified and protected.
paragraphs: {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} has a fixed 64-bit data stream transmitted continuously: 9 header bits (all ones), 40 data bits organized as 10 rows of 4 data bits plus 1 row-parity bit, 4 column-parity bits and 1 stop bit. There is no user-writable area. The ID is laser-programmed at the factory and cannot be changed.

{chip:atmel-t5577:name} organizes its {chip:atmel-t5577:memory.rewritable_bits}-bit EEPROM into page 0 (blocks 0–7) and page 1 (blocks 0–3). Block 0 on page 0 is the configuration block that sets modulation, data rate, bit count and other RF parameters. Blocks 1–7 store user data or format-emulation payloads. Block 7 can optionally hold a 32-bit password to protect write operations.
bullets: {chip:atmel-t5577:name} configuration block settings determine which legacy format the chip emulates. Changing block 0 switches the chip's over-the-air behavior without replacing hardware.
{chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} cards always transmit the same 64-bit frame on every interrogation. There is no session key, challenge-response or rolling code.
{chip:atmel-t5577:name} password protection prevents unauthorized writes but does not encrypt the read data. The emulated ID is still broadcast in the clear.

sections.title: How secure is it against cloning?
sections.intro: Both {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} and {chip:atmel-t5577:name} are fundamentally insecure by modern standards. Any attacker with a $20 Proxmark or similar 125 kHz reader/writer can capture and duplicate the transmitted ID in seconds.
bullets: {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} cloning requires only reading the 40-bit ID from the original card and writing it to a {chip:atmel-t5577:name} blank configured in {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} emulation mode.
{chip:atmel-t5577:name} password protection slows casual cloning but does not prevent it. The password is transmitted in plaintext during write operations and can be sniffed.
No 125 kHz chip supports mutual authentication, encrypted communication or cryptographic diversification.
B2B customers with any security requirement beyond basic identification should migrate to MIFARE DESFire, iCLASS SE or comparable 13.56 MHz platforms.

sections.title: How do you migrate from 125 kHz to 13.56 MHz?
sections.intro: For organizations with large 125 kHz installed bases, migration is typically phased. Dual-frequency readers and multi-technology cards ease the transition without a forklift replacement of all existing infrastructure.
bullets: Dual-frequency cards embed both a 125 kHz chip ({chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} or {chip:atmel-t5577:name}) and a 13.56 MHz chip ([MIFARE Classic](/guides/mifare-classic-1k-4k-chip-encyclopedia/), DESFire or iCLASS) in a single card body.
Dual-frequency readers detect and process both 125 kHz and 13.56 MHz cards, allowing old and new credentials to coexist during the migration window.
Migration timelines of 12–24 months are typical for mid-size enterprises with 500–5 000 cardholders.
{chip:atmel-t5577:name} cards can serve as interim credentials during migration because they can be reprogrammed to match multiple legacy reader formats across the facility.

sections.title: Why a $25 Proxmark trivially clones {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} and {chip:atmel-t5577:name} in the field
sections.intro: Both chips were designed in an era where no consumer-grade transceiver existed for 125 kHz. That assumption no longer holds. Off-the-shelf hardware such as the Proxmark3 RDV4, Flipper Zero, ChameleonMini, iCopy-X and even mass-market Chinese 'RFID copier' duplicators (sub-$25 on Amazon and AliExpress) can read an {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} ID in under one second and write it to a {chip:atmel-t5577:name} blank in another two. Security teams need to understand the workflow to plan credible mitigations.
bullets: Read phase — A nearby attacker sweeps the badge area at coffee-shop or elevator distance (5-15 cm with a stock antenna; up to 60 cm with an extended-range loop). The Proxmark `lf em 410x reader` command captures the 40-bit UID in one inductive cycle and stores it in onboard flash — no physical contact, no log entry on the panel side, no reader alarm.

Decode phase — The captured 64-bit frame (9 header bits + 40 UID bits + parity + 1 stop) is human-readable hex. Tools like Proxmark client, Iceman fork firmware, and the Flipper Zero 'lfrfid' app print the {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} UID in the same canonical format that downstream access control panels (HID Edge, Mercury MR52, S2 NetBox) accept on Wiegand-26.

Write phase — The attacker drops a $0.40 {chip:atmel-t5577:name} blank on the writer pad. The Proxmark `lf em 410x clone` (or `lf t55 wipe; lf em 410x_write`) sets {chip:atmel-t5577:name} block 0 configuration to {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} emulation (RF/64 Manchester, 40-bit data) and burns the captured UID into blocks 1-2. The cloned card is bit-identical to the original on every reader.

Counter-measures that actually work — Replace the credential, not just the reader: deploy {chip:nxp-mifare-desfire-ev3:short_name} (AES-128 + EAL5+) or HID Seos (AES-128 + Diffie-Hellman ECC + SIO wrapper) on dual-frequency cards so the existing 125 kHz reader population can be retired in waves. Until then, switch panels to OSDP v2 Secure Channel so the wire protocol can no longer be replayed even if the credential is sniffed.

Defense in depth that does not work — Adding a 32-bit {chip:atmel-t5577:name} write password protects only future writes; the broadcast UID stays in the clear. Embossed photo IDs, holograms and tamper labels do nothing against electronic cloning. CCTV at readers helps forensics but never prevents the first incident.

sections.title: Procurement decision framework for 125 kHz buyers in 2026
sections.intro: Despite 15 years of warnings, 125 kHz cards still ship in volume because installed-base inertia is real. The right purchase is the one that minimizes total cost of ownership while keeping a credible upgrade path open — not the cheapest sticker price. Use this framework when ordering replacement stock or refreshing a legacy site.
bullets: Choose {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} only when — The application has zero security model (animal ID per ISO 11784/11785, time-and-attendance with photo verification, asset tags inside locked cabinets) and unit cost is the sole purchase criterion. Volume {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} PVC cards land at $0.08-$0.15 in 1K+ quantities; clamshell badges $0.18-$0.30; epoxy keyfobs $0.20-$0.40 per unit DDP from China.

Choose {chip:atmel-t5577:name} (or compatible ATA5577 / {chip:em-microelectronic-em4305:short_name}) when — You need to consolidate multiple legacy reader formats (HID Prox 26-bit, Indala 27-bit, AWID, Kantech ioProx) onto one card SKU, run an interim phase during a 12-24 month migration to 13.56 MHz, or maintain a reservist stock for facilities you cannot upgrade in this budget cycle. {chip:atmel-t5577:name} PVC card cost runs $0.25-$0.50 in 1K volume.

Skip 125 kHz entirely when — The site has any access-controlled space holding cash, regulated data, controlled substances, weapons, hazardous chemicals, or critical infrastructure. Specify dual-frequency cards ({chip:atmel-t5577:name} + DESFire EV3 or {chip:atmel-t5577:name} + iCLASS Seos) so that the 125 kHz side handles legacy doors and the 13.56 MHz side handles the upgraded readers as panels and headends are replaced in parallel.

Vendor and chip-revision diligence — {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} originals are EM Microelectronic; second-source clones include Atmel TK4100, EM4102, and various unbranded 'EM-compatible' Chinese ICs. Quality varies; insist on factory test reports for read distance and bit-error rate. {chip:atmel-t5577:name} has been Microchip-owned since the Atmel acquisition; the legitimate part is Microchip ATA5577C. Watch for relabelled '{chip:atmel-t5577:name}' that are actually {chip:em-microelectronic-em4305:short_name} (different command set, no HID Prox emulation).

Logistics and lead time — A 10K-card {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} PVC order with custom artwork ships in 7-12 working days from a Shenzhen converter, $300-$800 plate fee one-time, EXW $0.10/card, DDP USA $0.13/card with sea freight. {chip:atmel-t5577:name} typically adds 2-3 days for chip lot allocation and runs $0.05-$0.10 per card premium over {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name}.

faq.question: Can a {chip:atmel-t5577:name} card replace any {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} card?
faq.answer: Yes. {chip:atmel-t5577:name} can be configured to emulate {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name}'s modulation, data rate and ID format. You program the desired 40-bit ID into the {chip:atmel-t5577:name}'s data blocks and set the configuration block to {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} mode. The reader cannot distinguish between a genuine {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} and a {chip:atmel-t5577:name} in emulation mode.

faq.question: Is {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} still a good choice for new deployments?
faq.answer: Only for applications with no security requirement and maximum cost sensitivity, such as animal identification tags or basic time-clock badges. For any access-control application, {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name}'s lack of authentication makes it unsuitable. Consider migrating to 13.56 MHz smart cards.

faq.question: What is the read range of {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} and {chip:atmel-t5577:name} cards?
faq.answer: Both operate at 125 kHz and achieve similar read ranges of 5–15 cm with standard proximity readers. Read range depends primarily on the reader's antenna size and transmit power, not the chip type.

faq.question: Can {chip:atmel-t5577:name} cards be locked to prevent reprogramming?
faq.answer: {chip:atmel-t5577:name} supports a 32-bit password that must be provided before write commands are accepted. However, this password is transmitted unencrypted over the air and can be captured with a sniffer. True tamper-proof locking is not possible with 125 kHz technology.

faq.question: If we standardize on {chip:atmel-t5577:name} for all new orders, can we drop {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} from our supply chain?
faq.answer: Yes — {chip:atmel-t5577:name} in {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} emulation mode is bit-identical to a real {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} from the reader's perspective, so you can phase out the older SKU without changing readers or panels. The only economic question is unit cost: a {chip:atmel-t5577:name} PVC card runs $0.25-$0.50 versus $0.08-$0.15 for {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name} in 1K-10K quantities, so consolidating saves logistics overhead but raises material spend roughly 2-3×. Most buyers consolidate when their site count exceeds 3-5 facilities or when they want a single SKU that can be reprogrammed in the field for one-off replacements.

faq.question: How does {chip:atmel-t5577:name} compare with {chip:em-microelectronic-em4305:short_name} for our use case?
faq.answer: Both are programmable 125 kHz chips, but they target different scenarios. {chip:atmel-t5577:name} (Microchip ATA5577) is the multi-format emulator: it can mimic {chip:em-microelectronic-em4100:short_name}, HID Prox 26-bit, Indala, AWID, FDX-B and similar legacy formats by changing its block 0 configuration word, which makes it the workhorse for access-control consolidation. {chip:em-microelectronic-em4305:short_name} has a richer command set with 32-bit password, anti-collision, and a true write-after-read protocol, which makes it preferred for animal ID applications under ISO 11784/11785 FDX-B and for industrial asset tags where the data payload changes over the asset's life. For pure access control consolidation, default to {chip:atmel-t5577:name}; for animal husbandry or mutable-data industrial tagging, default to {chip:em-microelectronic-em4305:short_name}.
